meta.title: Who really said "First, do no harm"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Hippocrates. The motto is in no Hippocratic text — Epidemics I says “to do good or to do no harm,” and the English maxim with its Latin dates to 1860.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'First, do no harm'?
meta.ogDescription: “First, do no harm” is not in the Hippocratic Oath. The nearest genuine line puts helping first. Scholars call the motto proverbial, not Hippocratic.

answer.label: Not Hippocrates — a later proverbial motto
answer.authorDates: Documented in medical print only from the 19th century · earliest English-plus-Latin form 1860
answer.sourceLine: The motto appears in no surviving Hippocratic text. The closest genuine line, in Of the Epidemics Book I, tells the physician to “have two special objects in view with regard to disease, namely, to do good or to do no harm” — helping first, not-harming as the fallback. The English maxim coupled with its Latin “Primum non nocere” is documented only from 1860, when Thomas Inman credited it to Thomas Sydenham.

source.heading: The nearest thing Hippocrates actually wrote

docMeta.dd: “First, do no harm” / “Primum non nocere” — found in no Hippocratic text
English maxim with its Latin, 1860 (per Cedric M. Smith, 2005); the bare Latin in print from 1816 (per Suss, 2024)

source.excerpt: With regard to the dangers of these cases, one must always attend to the seasonable concoction of all the evacuations, and to the favorable and critical abscesses… The physician must be able to tell the antecedents, know the present, and foretell the future — must mediate these things, and have two special objects in view with regard to disease, namely, to do good or to do no harm. The art consists in three things — the disease, the patient, and the physician.
trail: The Oath of Hippocrates in Adams’s translation ↗ never uses the word “harm”; the closest it comes is a promise to “abstain from whatever is deleterious and mischievous.”

The nearest genuine line is in Of the Epidemics, Book I ↗, where the physician is to “do good or to do no harm” — good first, harm-avoidance second. Wikiquote ↗ lists this passage among his sourced quotations and carries no entry for “First, do no harm.”

Clinical pharmacologist Cedric M. Smith searched writings back to the Middle Ages and found the English maxim coupled with its Latin only in 1860, attributed to Thomas Sydenham — a chain Wikipedia traces to Thomas Inman’s book of that year ↗.

A 2024 philological survey, Richard A. Suss, “First Do No Harm Is Proverbial, Not Hippocratic” ↗, examined over a hundred translations and found “no basis for the mottos in ancient medical authority.”
source.excerptNote: Note the order. Adams’s 1849 rendering makes doing good the first object and doing no harm the second; the popular motto inverts that ranking and drops the rest of the sentence.

sourceLink.text: Of the Epidemics, trans. Francis Adams (1849), at Wikisource

source.rightsNote: The motto itself has no identifiable author and no traceable first publication, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for it. The passage displayed above is a different matter: Francis Adams’s 1849 English translation of Of the Epidemics was published long before 1931 and is in the public domain in the United States, as is the ancient Greek original.

author.name: Hippocrates
author.heading: The man the motto was pinned on
author.metaLine: c. 460 BC – 377 BC · Greek physician of Kos, referred to as the father of medicine
author.bio: Hippocrates of Kos was a Greek physician of the fifth and fourth centuries BC, remembered as the father of medicine for treating disease as something with natural rather than divine causes. The sprawling body of texts that carries his name — the Hippocratic Corpus — was written by many hands over several centuries, which is part of why separating genuine Hippocratic sayings from later mottos is so difficult. His actual counsel about harm survives in Epidemics, and it puts helping the patient first and refraining from harm second — the opposite ranking to the motto now pinned on him.

misattribution.heading: Four origin stories, none of them holding
misattribution.intro: “First, do no harm” may be the most-quoted line in medicine and one of the least sourced. Several rival pedigrees circulate; here is what each one actually rests on.

items.why: The motto is simply not there. In Francis Adams’s translation of the Oath ↗ the word “harm” never occurs at all; the nearest promises are to “abstain from whatever is deleterious and mischievous” and to “abstain from every voluntary act of mischief and corruption” — both qualified by intent.

This is the genuine source of the idea, but not of the motto. The physician is told to “have two special objects in view with regard to disease, namely, to do good or to do no harm” (Adams, 1849 ↗). Doing good comes first; the motto puts it last.

items.scope: Thomas Inman, Foundation for a New Theory and Practice of Medicine (1860)
items.why: On Cedric M. Smith’s 2005 reckoning, Inman’s 1860 book is the earliest place the English maxim and a Latin form appear together, credited to Sydenham — who had been dead for well over a century. Smith searched writings back to the Middle Ages and found nothing earlier; Suss’s 2024 survey ↗ reports that the Sydenham attribution offers “no written primary sources,” and its Box 17 prints the bare Latin “Primum non nocere” from Boyer in 1816 onward — so 1860 is the earliest English-plus-Latin pairing, not the earliest Latin. Inman’s own Latin, Suss notes, reads “Primum est ut non nocere.”

items.scope: Elisha Bartlett (1844) and Worthington Hooker, Physician and Patient (1847)
items.why: Bartlett called it “the golden axiom of Chomel” and Hooker passed the credit on, but the axiom was reportedly part of Chomel’s spoken teaching, and Hooker “used neither the specific expression, nor the traditional Latin phrase” ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: No author, no first publication, several competing wordings and a borrowed pedigree: on the evidence, “First, do no harm” is a proverb rather than a quotation ↗ — a good rule of thumb that acquired an ancient signature it never earned.

context.heading: Why the wrong version stuck
lead: Medicine has always needed a short way to say “the treatment can be worse than the disease,” and “First, do no harm” is a very good four-word version of that. It is also a rule about priority: harm-avoidance first, benefit second. That ranking is what makes the motto quotable — and it is exactly the part Hippocrates did not write.

In Of the Epidemics the instruction runs the other way round: the physician should aim “to do good or to do no harm.” Do good; failing that, at least do no damage. Richard A. Suss’s 2024 survey of more than a hundred translations of the Oath and the Epidemics maxim concluded that the mottos “turn classical authority on its head” and that there is “no basis for the mottos in ancient medical authority” ↗.
context.detailsSummary: How a proverb acquires a pedigree
detailsBody: The paper trail is short and it runs backwards from the present, not forwards from antiquity. Elisha Bartlett’s Essay on the Philosophy of Medical Science (1844) credits “the golden axiom of Chomel” — the Parisian clinician Auguste François Chomel — with the idea that doing good is only the second law of therapeutics, the first being not to do harm. Worthington Hooker repeated the credit in Physician and Patient (1847), but, as Wikipedia’s account of the phrase notes ↗, Hooker “used neither the specific expression, nor the traditional Latin phrase.”

Sixteen years after Bartlett, Thomas Inman’s Foundation for a New Theory and Practice of Medicine (1860) put the English maxim and a Latin aphorism together and hung them on Thomas Sydenham, dead since 1689. Cedric M. Smith, searching writings back to the Middle Ages, found nothing earlier — which makes 1860 Smith’s date for the English-plus-Latin pairing, not for the Latin itself. Suss’s Box 17 prints “Primum non nocere” in medical books from Boyer in 1816 onward, and records that Inman’s own Latin was the looser “Primum est ut non nocere.” Suss also checked the Sydenham and Chomel attributions for primary evidence and reported that neither gives any written source from those physicians or their followers. What is left is a proverb: no author, many wordings, and a borrowed pedigree.
context.pull: Hippocrates said do good, or failing that do no harm. The motto swapped the order and kept his name.

schema.webPageName: Who really said 'First, do no harm'?

sourcesVerified.claim: The phrase does not appear in the Hippocratic Oath; the closest approximation in the Hippocratic Corpus is in Epidemics ("to do good or to do no harm", trans. Adams); Hooker's 1847 Physician and Patient credited the axiom to Chomel but "used neither the specific expression, nor the traditional Latin phrase"; Hooker was quoting Elisha Bartlett's 1844 Essay on the Philosophy of Medical Science ("the golden axiom of Chomel"); Cedric M. Smith's April 2005 Journal of Clinical Pharmacology investigation traced the expression and its Latin phrase to an attribution to Thomas Sydenham in Thomas Inman's 1860 Foundation for a New Theory and Practice of Medicine.

Francis Adams's 1849 translation of Of the Epidemics, Book I, contains: "The physician must be able to tell the antecedents, know the present, and foretell the future- must mediate these things, and have two special objects in view with regard to disease, namely, to do good or to do no harm. The art consists in three things-the disease, the patient, and the physician." The page header names Francis Adams as translator and states "Translated in 1849."

The full Adams translation of the Oath of Hippocrates contains no occurrence of the word "harm" and no phrase resembling "first, do no harm"; its nearest wordings are "abstain from whatever is deleterious and mischievous" and "abstain from every voluntary act of mischief and corruption."

Wikiquote lists among Hippocrates's sourced quotations the Epidemics Book I maxim ("As to diseases, make a habit of two things — to help, or at least, to do no harm", with variant translation "...to do good or to do no harm"), gives his dates as c. 460 BC - 377 BC and describes him as "referred to as the 'father of medicine'", and carries no entry for the wording "First, do no harm". The Oath section reproduces the Francis Adams translation.

Richard A. Suss, "First Do No Harm Is Proverbial, Not Hippocratic" (OSF Preprints, 21 November 2024): "An extensive survey of translations and commentary finds no basis for the mottos in ancient medical authority. Instead they apparently developed proverbially." The synopsis states the mottos "do not reflect words or meanings in the Hippocratic Oath", that "the mottos turn classical authority on its head", and that "Attributions to the English and French physicians Thomas Sydenham and Auguste François Chomel give no written primary sources related to them or from any of their followers as credible witnesses."

Cedric M. Smith, "Origin and uses of primum non nocere--above all, do no harm!", Journal of Clinical Pharmacology 45, no. 4 (April 2005): 371-377. Abstract: "It has been reported that the author was neither Hippocrates nor Galen. Searches of writings back to the Middle Ages have uncovered the appearance of the axiom as expressed in English, coupled with its unique Latin, in 1860, with attribution to the English physician, Thomas Sydenham."

A site search of Quote Investigator for "harm" returns no article on "First, do no harm", "primum non nocere", or Hippocrates — i.e. QI has not published an investigation of this quotation, so there is no QI anchor finding to defer to.
